Clause 6 deserves emphasis because it is the clause conventional records come closest to and still miss. A conventional record asks what happens if the component fails. An AI record asks what happens when the component succeeds and is wrong, which is the more common and far more expensive case, because a failure is loud and a confident wrong answer is silent.

### A worked record, compressed

**Healthcare, prior authorization evidence assembly.**

| Field | Entry |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | Assemble the payer policy criteria and the supporting chart excerpts at order entry, as a workflow with a clinical review gate |
| Alternatives | Agentic retrieval with autonomous submission, rejected on restraint. Deterministic rules over structured fields only, rejected because 60 percent of supporting evidence is in narrative notes |
| Criterion | Escape rate no worse than the current process at 1.2 percent, cycle time under 3 days, no submission without clinical sign-off |
| **Model dependency** | Sonnet-class, pinned, assumed 12 month support, migration owner is the clinical systems platform lead, runway 8 weeks including revalidation |
| **Non-determinism tolerance** | Excerpt selection may vary between runs. The cited chart locations must be exact and are validated structurally. The policy identifier must be deterministic and is resolved by lookup, not generation |
| **Eval gate** | 400 case set, segmented by payer and service line, 95 percent citation validity and 90 percent criterion coverage per segment, run by the clinical informatics team, blocks promotion |
| **Human oversight** | Pre-action approval by a clinical reviewer before submission. Handoff package is the criteria list, the cited excerpts with links and the single question "does this evidence support the indication" |
| **Data egress** | Protected health information leaves the electronic health record into the enterprise gateway, processed under a business associate agreement, retained 30 days in the audit sink, no vendor training use ⚠ |
| **Failure mode and blast radius** | A missed criterion produces a denial and a resubmission. Detection at denial, roughly 6 days. Up to 400 cases affected before detection at current volume, mitigated by a daily denial-reason monitor |
| **Reversal path and switching condition** | Configuration flag reverts to manual assembly with no deployment, under 5 minutes. Prior release tuple retained for 90 days. The condition that would reopen the decision: citation validity below 90 percent on any payer segment for two consecutive weeks, or a payer withdrawing acceptance of assembled evidence |

Note that every clause is answerable in one or two lines. The record's value is not its length, it is that seven questions with expensive answers were asked before the build rather than after.

## 2.10 Portfolio-level architecture

One AI system is a design problem. Forty AI systems is a portfolio problem, and the two have opposite failure modes. A single system fails by being under-engineered. A portfolio fails by being over-shared: a central team builds abstractions that every team must adopt, adoption stalls, teams route around the platform and the estate fragments anyway, now with an unused platform to maintain as well.

```
  THE FLEET, drawn as obligation rather than as boxes
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
   sys A    sys B    sys C    sys D    sys E    sys F   ... sys N
     |        |        |        |        |        |          |
     +--------+--------+---+----+--------+--------+----------+
                           |
              == MANDATORY WAIST ============================
                 gateway  |  identity + secrets  |  audit sink
              ===============================================
                           |
              -- OPTIONAL SHOULDERS ------------------------
                 model routing | prompt & asset registry
                 eval harness  | retrieval layer
              ---------------------------------------------
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Above the waist: domain prompts, evals, rubrics, corpora.
  Never shared. Sharing them is what stalls adoption.
```

**The three drawn here are the irreducible core, not the whole mandatory set.** 1.6's standards table makes six things mandatory: these three plus data egress boundaries, the eval gate before production and the dependency register entry. The difference is not a disagreement about what is required. **The three drawn are the three the platform must operate as shared services**, so they belong in a fleet diagram; the other three are obligations discharged at each system and enforced through the gateway and the release gate rather than run centrally. **Read 1.6's six as the mandatory set and these three as the part of it that has to exist before any of the rest can be enforced.**

### The seven shared services

| Service | What it does | Share by default? | What premature sharing costs | The trigger to share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Gateway** | Single egress path for model traffic, with policy, rate control, key management and per-request identity | **Mandatory** | Almost nothing. The interface is narrow and stable | Day one. This is the control point that makes everything else possible |
| **Identity and secrets** | Who is calling, on whose behalf, with what credentials and what scope | **Mandatory** | Nothing. Never let a team solve this locally | Day one |
| **Audit sink** | Immutable capture of requests, responses, model identifiers, trace identifiers and identities | **Mandatory** | Nothing, provided the schema is permissive | Day one. Retrofitting an audit trail loses the correlation identifiers |
| **Model routing** | Selecting model and tier by task class, with fallback | Optional | High if premature. Routing policy is task-specific, and a shared router encodes the first consumer's task shape | Three systems with genuinely similar task classes |
| **Prompt and asset registry** | Versioned storage, ownership, dependency links | Optional, strongly recommended | Low. Registry is storage and metadata, not enforcement | Second system, or the first time a prompt is consumed by two systems |
| **Eval harness** | Running sets, scoring, reporting, gating | Optional, strongly recommended | Moderate if the harness prescribes grader design. The runner should be shared, the sets never | Second system. Share the runner immediately, never the sets |
| **Retrieval layer** | Chunking, indexing, ranking, permission filtering | Optional, often wrong | **Highest of all.** Chunking is selected by the corpus and indexing by the query pattern, so a shared layer either exposes every knob and saves nothing or hides them and is wrong for most corpora | Three systems with the same corpus shape and the same permission model. This is rarer than it sounds |

### The three sharing tests

Apply before elevating anything to a shared service.

1. **Is the interface stable across consumers?** If consumer two needs a parameter consumer one does not, the interface is not stable and you are about to build a configuration surface rather than a service.
2. **Does a defect in it mean the same thing to every consumer?** An outage in the gateway means the same thing to everyone. A recall regression in a shared retrieval layer means something different in every corpus, and nobody owns the fix.
3. **Would a consumer be blocked waiting for it?** If yes, do not share yet. A shared service that gates delivery converts the platform team into a queue.

**The decision rule: share when the interface is stable, the defects are common and nobody is blocked, and until all three hold let teams duplicate.**

Duplication is cheap and reversible. Premature abstraction is expensive and sticky, and it is paid for in the currency the platform team can least afford, which is adoption. Give this a name and use it in the room: **the shared-service queue tax**. Every mandatory shared service adds a coordination cost to every consumer, and if the service does not remove more work than the coordination costs, the platform is a net negative that is very hard to unwind.

### What must never be shared

| Never shared | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Eval sets** | They are the definition of correct for one task. A shared set measures nothing well. One eval set per architecture, and per system |
| **Prompts as running artifacts** | Share them as library assets to copy, never as a live dependency. A shared live prompt means one team's tuning is another team's incident |
| **Business rules** | A rule with two owners has no owner. Rules belong to the function accountable for them |
| **Corpora with different permission models** | Merging two corpora merges their access control, and the merge is always to the looser model unless someone does the work |

**Worked example, financial services.** A bank stood up a platform team that built a shared retrieval service, a shared prompt service and a shared agent framework before it had three consumers. Fourteen months later there were four production systems, three of which had bypassed the retrieval service because it could not do the chunking their corpus needed, and two of which had forked the agent framework. The platform team was maintaining three services with a combined consumer count of two. The recovery was to withdraw the retrieval and agent services, keep the gateway and the registry, mandate the audit sink and let the four teams keep their own retrieval. Delivery velocity roughly doubled in the following quarter and the estate became more governable rather than less, because the mandatory waist was now short enough that nobody had a reason to route around it.

### Sequencing a portfolio, and the second system problem

An estate is never designed as a portfolio. It accumulates one system at a time, in whatever order sponsorship produced, and its shared surface is decided long before anyone says portfolio. **The first system establishes nothing, because it has no peer.** Every choice in it is local and defensible, and no convention exists because there is nothing yet to be consistent with. Treating system one as a template is how one team's accidents become an enterprise standard.

**The second system is the decision point.** Whatever the second team does with the first team's choices becomes the estate's convention, written down or not. If system two joins the existing gateway, uses the same trace identifier and the same asset naming, the third inherits a convention and the fourth arrives into one. If system two re-solves those things, the estate has learned that re-solving is normal, and every later team will do the same and be right to.

What to standardize at system two is a short list: the mandatory waist above, the naming and metadata conventions for assets and the eval harness runner, never the sets. Leave alone everything above the waist: chunking, prompts, rubrics, business rules, tool surfaces, model tier and review placement. Those are properties of a use case, and standardizing them on a sample of two encodes the first system's accidents as policy. The three sharing tests keep the list short: at system two almost nothing passes the first test, because two consumers cannot demonstrate a stable interface.

Portfolios fail in three shapes, each with a detection signal available before the failure is expensive.

| Shape | What it is | Detection signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The estate of one-offs** | Every system solved gateway, logging, eval tooling and asset storage locally, so nothing is governable in one place | No identifier correlates a request across two systems, and a second-line question about model usage returns a different answer per system |
| **The premature platform** | Shared services stood up ahead of demand, each with more maintainers than consumers | Consumer count is below the headcount maintaining the service, and its roadmap is written by the platform team rather than requested by a consumer |
| **The accidental monolith** | One successful system accretes unrelated use cases because it is the only thing approved | Intake routes new requests to a system by name rather than by fit, and the eval set has grown segments sharing no failure mode |

The second is the failure the worked example above describes; the third looks like success while it happens, because usage is rising.

Sequencing follows. The roadmap material in 9.2 orders items by dependency and by political capital; the portfolio addition is narrower. **Order the early systems by what each one teaches, because systems two and three are paying for a capability that system four onward will use.** If system two runs over the same corpus, under the same permission model and with the same oversight placement as system one, it has cost a delivery slot and taught the estate nothing. Choose the second to exercise the entitlement model against a different corpus shape; choose the third to exercise a different oversight placement or route. Business value still selects what is worth building; between candidates of similar value, coverage is the better tiebreak.

⧉ **The retirement question is the one nobody asks at portfolio level: what happens to a shared service when its last consumer leaves.** Shared services do not retire on their own. Consumers migrate away one at a time, each departure individually rational, and the service persists with a maintainer, an on-call rotation, a patching obligation and a change process. A shared service with one consumer is a liability rather than an asset: it carries the shared-service queue tax named above and delivers no reuse. The remedy is unglamorous. Fold it back into its remaining consumer and delete the interface.

That gives the sharing rule an exit clause to match its entry tests. Share when the interface is stable, the defects are common and nobody is blocked. Withdraw when the consumer count falls to one and does not recover within two quarters, and set that floor when the service is created rather than arguing it while a team defends its own work. The bank above made this decision under duress, fourteen months in and after the estate had already routed around the platform. The same decision on a pre-agreed floor is a routine withdrawal rather than a reorganization.

## 2.11 Model portfolio strategy

Treat the model as **a dependency you do not control**. You do not set its version, its behavior, its pricing or its retirement date. No other component in an enterprise architecture has that profile, and conventional dependency management does not account for it, because a library you have vendored keeps working and a model endpoint does not.

### The four postures

| Posture | What it means | Buys you | Costs you | Fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Single vendor, single model** | One model for everything | Simplicity, deep optimization, one eval baseline, one set of behaviors to learn | Cost inefficiency on easy tasks, a single point of deprecation, no negotiating position | Early portfolios, under roughly ten systems |
| **Single vendor, multi-model** | Tiered use within one vendor's family | Real cost and latency optimization with one integration surface, one set of semantics for caching and tools | Still one vendor deprecation calendar | The common correct answer for most enterprises |
| **Multi-vendor, active-passive** | Primary vendor, second qualified and periodically exercised | Genuine continuity, a negotiating position, an answer to a concentration-risk question | Two integrations, two eval baselines and a fallback that decays unless exercised | Regulated environments with concentration-risk obligations ⚠ |
| **Multi-vendor, active-active** | Live traffic across vendors by task | Best cost and capability fit per task | Highest complexity, every prompt behaves differently on every model, eval cost multiplies by vendor count | Rarely justified. Usually a symptom of unresolved procurement |

**The decision rule: pick the simplest posture that satisfies your continuity obligation, and remember that a fallback nobody has exercised in six months is not a fallback.**

### Routing, cascades and the acceptance test per segment

A mixed-model design takes one of two shapes, and they are not variants of each other. **A router classifies the request up front and sends it to a model. A cascade tries the cheaper model and escalates on a signal.** The posture table above says which models are in the estate; this says how a request finds one.

| Shape | What it pays | Where it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Router** | A classification call on every request, its latency and the cost of maintaining the classifier | It inherits the classifier's error. A misrouted hard case is answered by the weak model and nothing notices |
| **Cascade** | The cheap call twice on every escalation: once wasted, once as the base of the expensive attempt | It doubles latency on exactly the hard cases, where the user is already waiting longest |

The cascade's escalation signal is the whole design. It must be a fact about the run rather than an opinion from the model: a schema validation failure, a retrieval returning nothing above threshold, a required field left empty, disagreement between two independent passes. **The model's self-reported confidence is not an escalation signal**, for the mechanical reason developed in 2.12, and the failure is specific to cascades: the signal reads high on precisely the cases the cascade exists to catch, so the escalation rate looks healthy while the cases that needed escalating did not get it.

What makes either shape defensible is the same discipline. **The cheaper model is accepted per segment, not in aggregate, measured on the harness.** An aggregate decision, the cheap model scores within two points of the expensive one overall, is dominated by the easy majority, which is the segment the cheap model handles best. The segments where it lags are small enough to disappear into the average and are, reliably, the segments with the highest cost of a wrong answer. Accepting in aggregate therefore routes the hardest segment to the weakest model and produces a system whose measured quality is fine and whose worst outcomes are worse than before. Run the comparison segmented, admit the cheap model only where it clears the threshold and leave the rest routed to the capable model until evidence says otherwise.

The governance consequence follows. **The routing rule is a configuration item with a named owner and a change record**, because a routing change alters system behavior as thoroughly as a prompt change does and reaches every request rather than one. It belongs in the change table in 8.6 at the row for a model change, gated on segmented evaluation: a threshold adjusted in a config file by whoever was on call is an ungoverned model swap for the population that crossed it.

### Abstraction layers and their real cost

An abstraction layer over model vendors is the standard architectural reflex and it has three costs that are routinely omitted from the proposal.

| Cost | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **The lowest common denominator tax** | The abstraction can only expose what every vendor supports. You lose the features that made a model worth choosing: caching semantics, tool-calling formats, thinking and effort controls, structured output enforcement, batch behavior. You have abstracted away the differentiation you were paying for |
| **Eval multiplication** | Every model you claim to support must be evaluated on every task, on every release, or the claim is unfounded. Two vendors and thirty systems is sixty eval baselines to maintain |
| **False confidence** | Portability that has never been executed is an assertion. Teams behave as if switching is cheap, defer the migration work and discover the real cost during the deprecation window |

**The decision rule: abstract at the boundary you will actually cross, evaluate every model you claim to support, and if you will not pay the eval cost then admit you support one model and pin it.**

A thin abstraction at the gateway, giving you a policy, identity and logging boundary plus the ability to redirect traffic, is almost always correct. A thick abstraction that normalizes prompt formats, tool schemas and response handling across vendors is almost always a mistake, and it is a mistake that gets more expensive to remove every quarter.

### Model deprecation as a standing architectural risk

**⧉ The single biggest gap in enterprise AI architecture is that every system in the portfolio has a hard dependency with a vendor-set expiry date, and in most organizations nobody owns the migration for any of them.** This is not a risk that materializes gradually. It arrives as a dated notice covering the whole estate at once, and the work is per system because behavior changes are per task. An organization with forty systems, no dependency register and a six month notice has a portfolio-scale emergency that will be discovered by whichever team happens to read the notice.

**The model dependency register.** One row per system, maintained centrally, populated from clause 1 of every decision record.

| Field | Why |
| --- | --- |
| System identifier and business owner | Who is affected and who decides |
| Model identifier and pinned version | The dependency itself |
| Announced or assumed end of support | The deadline |
| Eval set reference and current baseline score | What "still works" means for this system |
| Migration owner | A named person, not a team |
| Runway estimate | Engineering days plus revalidation plus any regulatory review ⚠ |
| Fallback model, and the date it was last exercised | Whether continuity is real |
| Downstream consumers assuming output stability | Who breaks if the output shape shifts |

**Pinning and its expiry.** Pinning a model version is correct and it is not a control on its own. A pin freezes behavior until the pinned version is retired, at which point the freeze becomes the problem: you have deferred all behavioral change to a single forced date with no runway. **A pin without an expiry date and a named owner is a deferral, not a control.** Every pin should carry a review date well ahead of the vendor's retirement date, and the review should ask whether the migration has been rehearsed.

**Regression on upgrade.** A newer, more capable model can be worse for your specific task, and the ways it goes wrong are systematic rather than random.

| Regression class | What breaks |
| --- | --- |
| **Format drift** | Output shape shifts subtly and a downstream parser that was never strict enough starts failing on a minority of cases |
| **Verbosity drift** | Longer or shorter outputs change cost, latency and any length-sensitive downstream logic |
| **Refusal boundary shift** | Content the previous model handled is now declined, or the reverse. Both are defects and the second is worse |
| **Tool-calling behavior** | Different propensity to call tools, different argument construction, different recovery from tool errors. Agentic systems feel this hardest |
| **Prompt sensitivity** | Instructions tuned against the old model's quirks stop earning their keep, and the prompt is now longer than it needs to be for no benefit |

The control is the eval gate, run per system, segmented, before any model change reaches production. This is the stage-gate rule applied at portfolio scale: evaluations gate any model swap, and at forty systems that means forty gates, which is exactly why the eval harness is a shared service and the eval sets are not.

**Worked example, financial services.** An insurer had 30 AI systems across underwriting, claims and servicing, all on two pinned models, none registered. A deprecation notice with a nine month horizon triggered an inventory. Eleven systems passed their eval sets on the successor model with no change. Fourteen needed prompt work, mostly format and verbosity drift against strict downstream parsers. Three had no eval set at all and could not be assessed, so they were migrated on a shadow deployment with manual comparison over four weeks. Two, both in a regulated underwriting path, required model change notification to the supervisor and consumed the entire runway. ⚠ Whether a model change is notifiable is a regulatory determination and belongs to the compliance function, not the architecture team. The lesson the insurer wrote down: the three systems with no eval set cost more than the other twenty-seven combined.

## 2.12 Human in the loop as an architecture

A human control is a component with a throughput, a latency, a failure rate and a cost. As a checkbox, it appears in the diagram, satisfies review and does nothing.

```
  THE FIVE PLACEMENTS, positioned against the action
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
                 model output        ACTION        consequence
                       |               |               |
   1 PRE-ACTION   [ human ]---------->|                |
     APPROVAL      blocks             |                |
                                      |                |
   2 POST-ACTION                      |--->[ human ]-->|  undo
     REVIEW                           |     reviews    |  window
                                      |                |
   3 SAMPLED                          |------------>[ n% ]---->
     AUDIT                            |          detective only
                                      |                |
   4 ESCALATION   [ signal? ]--yes-->[ human ]         |
     ON UNCERTAINTY    |--no-------------------------->|
                                      |                |
   5 EXCEPTION    [ rule flags ]-yes->[ human ]        |
     ONLY              |--no-------------------------->|
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  1 and 4 and 5 are preventive. 2 is corrective and needs a real
  undo window. 3 is detective and is not a safety control.
```

### The five placements compared

| Placement | Where it sits | Latency added | Throughput ceiling | Control strength | Characteristic failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Pre-action approval** | Blocks the action | Full reviewer queue time, hours to days | Reviewer capacity, hard | Strongest: nothing happens without a person | Rubber-stamping under queue pressure, degrading when most loaded |
| **Post-action review** | After the action, inside an undo window | None to the user | Reviewer capacity, asynchronous | Only as strong as the undo; none if the action is irreversible | Applied to irreversible actions, like anything already sent to a client |
| **Sampled audit** | A percentage, after the fact | None | Very high, scaling with the rate | Detective: measures the system, not the case | Presented as a safety control; a quality instrument, nothing else |
| **Escalation on uncertainty** | Routes on a signal | Only for escalated cases | High, if the escalation rate is low | Strong where the signal is sound | Routing on the model's uncalibrated self-reported confidence; route on structural signals |
| **Exception only** | A deterministic rule picks what a human sees | Only for flagged cases | Highest of the preventive placements | Strong for the flagged class, zero for the unflagged | The failure nobody wrote a rule for is invisible by construction |

**The decision rule: place a preventive human control on every irreversible or high-stakes action, sample the rest, and never let a sampled audit be called the control that makes an irreversible action safe.**

One variant matters because professional work runs on it: **the human in the middle**, editing and issuing the draft rather than approving a system action. It scales best for professional work, keeps accountability clear and is pre-action.

**A second variant matters because agentic work runs on it: plan-level approval.** Instead of gating each action an agent takes, the reviewer approves the trajectory before execution begins, and the agent then runs it. The placement is still pre-action, and the unit of review has changed from the step to the plan.

The argument for it is not convenience. **Per-step approval degrades into non-review at a rate that scales with the number of steps**, and the mechanism has a name worth using in a design conversation: **consent fatigue**, the collapse of oversight when a reviewer is asked to approve so many actions in sequence that they approve without reading. It is the same failure as rubber-stamping in 4.6, arriving through a different door: not queue pressure across cases, but prompt volume within a single case. A reviewer asked to approve forty actions to complete one task is not performing forty reviews. ⚠ Anthropic's published work on agent autonomy reports that requiring sign-off on every action adds friction without a proportionate safety gain, and favors a person monitoring the run and intervening over a person consenting to each step; the current framing should be verified against the published research rather than cited from here.

**Where it belongs, and where it does not.** Plan-level approval fits work whose plan is legible before execution and whose steps are individually low-consequence, which is most agentic engineering and analysis work. **It does not substitute for a gate on an irreversible or high-stakes individual action**, and the two compose rather than compete: approve the plan, and still gate the one step inside it that moves money, sends something external or cannot be undone. The failure to avoid is treating plan approval as blanket authorization for whatever the run turns out to contain, which is how a reviewed plan becomes an unreviewed action.

**The reviewer-view requirement carries over unchanged and is easy to lose here.** Approving a plan requires seeing the plan, the inputs it was formed from and the reason review was triggered. A plan presented as a list of intended actions with no basis is the same defect as an output presented with no source, and it produces the same approval.

### Routing by risk

On placement 4 the signal matters more than the placement: which cases reach a person is the architectural question, and with finite capacity, where to spend it.

| Route to a human when | Because |
| --- | --- |
| Value exceeds a threshold | Error cost scales with value |
| Source material is ambiguous or internally contradictory | The system has no good answer |
| Confidence is low, against a **calibrated** threshold | The calibration is the load-bearing part |
| The pattern is novel | Novel patterns are where systematic errors begin |
| The decision affects a person's rights or entitlements | Regulatory expectation and accountability |
| Policy is silent | Silence is exactly what a person is for |

**Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is unusable as a routing signal**, the third row's load-bearing condition: poorly calibrated for mechanical reasons, confidently wrong on the hard cases where the signal was needed, usable only after comparison against a labeled set with derived thresholds. Route instead on structural signals, pipeline facts rather than model opinion: retrieval returning nothing above threshold, a missing required field, a value outside a known range, a schema validation failure, disagreement between two independent passes, an amount above a limit.

Four reliable escalation triggers: an explicit request for a human, honored immediately; a policy gap rather than a merely hard case; inability to progress; ambiguity about identity or entitlement, where the move is to ask not guess. Two unreliable: the user seems annoyed, and the model's confidence.

### Reviewer fatigue, automation bias and the calibration problem

Three human factors, compounding.

| Factor | What it is | Design response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fatigue** | Detection quality falls with volume and session length: a reviewer on their 200th item is a different instrument from their 5th | Cap batch sizes and session length. Rotate. Model reviewer capacity in the sizing model as a real constraint, at the fatigue-adjusted rather than fresh rate |
| **Automation bias** | People accept a confident machine output more readily than the same claim from a colleague, and more so as its track record improves | Never default to approve. No bulk approve on gated actions. Present the claim to be checked, not the document. Require an explicit action per item |
| **Calibration** | Whether the reviewer's approve and reject decisions track actual correctness | Measure it directly. The hard one, and the one skipped |

**A reviewer who approves 99 percent of items is not a control unless you know the base rate.** At 99 percent system correctness that rate is right; at 85 percent the reviewer is a rubber stamp and the control decorative. It therefore cannot be evaluated without the eval harness, the joint the two disciplines meet at and where most oversight designs quietly fall apart.

### Designing the handoff package

Reviewer decision quality is set by what you put in front of them: six elements, omissions mattering as much as inclusions.

| Element | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| **The specific decision, as a question** | "Does this evidence support the indication?" not "review this." A reviewer given an artifact reviews it; given a question, answers it |
| **The claim to be checked, isolated** | Not the whole output: the two or three assertions whose wrongness would matter, each next to its source |
| **The source, directly linked** | Deep link to the passage, page or record; navigation time is attention spent on logistics |
| **What the system did not find** | Absent evidence, failed lookups, low-scoring retrievals: what a reviewer cannot reconstruct and most needs |
| **The actions, with consequences stated** | "Approve and submit to payer" not "approve." The reviewer should not have to remember what the button does |
| **A time budget** | The design's assumed seconds per item, in the capacity model. Real time triple that means the control is under-resourced and degrading |

An escalation is a takeover mid-process rather than review of a proposed output, so whoever takes over needs a structured summary: who, the issue, what has been established, the recommended action and why. **A raw transcript is not a handoff**: documentation with a very short deadline.

Self-reported confidence is not a routing input: show it if it helps, never let it decide what the reader sees.

### Measuring whether the human control works

Four measures. Anything less and you have an assumption.

| Measure | How | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Seeded-defect catch rate** | Inject known defective items into the queue at a low rate and count the catches | The only direct measure of control effectiveness; all else is a proxy ⚠ Seeding into a live regulated queue needs an agreed protocol and sign-off first |
| **Override rate against a measured base rate** | Compare the reviewer's rejection rate to the measured error rate on the same population | Detects rubber-stamping and over-rejection, neither visible from the rate alone |
| **Time on task per item** | Instrument the review interface | A median well below the design assumption means review is not happening; well above means an inadequate package |
| **Downstream escape rate** | Defects reaching the customer or record after review | The outcome measure, compared against the pre-AI escape rate the workflow survey gave you |

Add inter-reviewer agreement where two reviewers run the same items: low agreement means an underspecified rubric and a control measuring reviewers, not outputs.

**Worked example, healthcare.** A payer ran AI-assisted clinical coding with pre-action approval by certified coders: approval at 97 percent, the program reported high quality. Seeded-defect testing at 2 percent injection found a 41 percent catch rate and a median 11 seconds on task against a design assumption of 90. The cause was the handoff package: coders saw the full note and proposed codes, new versus carried-forward codes unisolated and the supporting text unindicated. Showing only changed codes with the supporting passage highlighted took the catch rate to 88 percent and the median to 47 seconds, at a throughput cost of about 20 percent: the control's real price, which the organization had not been paying and not getting.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question.** At the threshold you just set, what is the arrival rate into the review queue, and is the reviewer pool sized for it at 2am?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setting the calibrated confidence threshold | Modeling arrival rate, review time, queue depth and headcount first | Capacity and staffing plan, operations |
| Pre-action approval on high-value cases | Out-of-hours coverage and the service level for a paused transaction | Rota and escalation matrix, operations |
| Treating human review as the control | Measuring reviewer override rate and agreement against a gold set | Reviewer quality report, the quality lead |
| Designing the handoff package | Retention and evidentiary format of the review record | Retention schedule, the records function |

**What this costs the organization.** The gate is recurring headcount scaling with volume, so a threshold without a queue model produces the backlog it exists to prevent. The forgotten cost is automation bias: a reviewer approving the draft rather than reaching their own answer is a control you pay for and do not have.

**The executive translation.** The human gate is a standing headcount commitment priced per reviewed case, against what the errors it prevents cost us today.

## 2.13 Memory architecture at enterprise scale

Memory is the most under-designed component in enterprise AI systems, because it arrives as a product feature rather than an architectural decision and it creates obligations the moment it is switched on.

### The four memory questions

| Question | Why it is architectural |
| --- | --- |
| **What is remembered?** | Preferences and working state are cheap. Facts about people, matters, cases or clients are regulated data the instant they are written |
| **For whom?** | The principal the memory is scoped to. User, team, matter, client, tenant or global. This is the contamination boundary |
| **For how long?** | Retention is a policy decision, not a storage default. "Until deleted" is not a retention period |
| **Who can cause it to be forgotten, and does that reach derived copies?** | Erasure must reach the memory store, any embeddings of it, any summaries built from it and any evaluation data drawn from it |

**The decision rule: scope memory to the smallest principal that makes it useful, default to the session and require an explicit decision with a named owner to widen the scope.**

### The write policy is the architecture

Memory design conversations concentrate on retrieval and storage: which store, which key, which embedding. They skip the decision that determines everything downstream, which is what earns a write. **A memory system is defined by its write policy rather than its storage technology: the write policy fixes the contents and every other component only moves them around.**

The distinction from retrieval is sharper than the comparison below makes it look. Retrieval answers from a corpus somebody curated, where every chunk has an owner and a source of record behind it. Memory answers from a record the system wrote about itself, unreviewed at the moment of writing. **Memory is the only store in the architecture whose contents the system authored**, so provenance, review, authority and supersession are manufactured by the write path or they are absent.

Four candidate policies. The choice is usually inherited from a product default.

| Write policy | Precision | Review burden | Erasure exposure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Write everything** | None. A transcript renamed | Unbounded, growing with traffic | Maximal. Everything said sits under a second retention clock |
| **On explicit user instruction** | Highest. The principal asserted it matters | Small, inspectable case by case | Low. The individual can enumerate their entries |
| **On a model judgment of durability** | Unmeasured until sampled and graded | Moderate, but a judgment review not a content review | Unpredictable. What is held is the model's opinion of what mattered |
| **Only structured facts a schema admits** | Enforced at the boundary | Schema review once, then exceptions | Lowest. A field-level operation with a known blast radius |

The fourth is the only one that delivers the per-individual enumerability erasure depends on, per the memory row in 4.11. It buys that by refusing to remember what the schema did not anticipate, a real cost and a defensible one.

**An unbounded write policy produces a store nobody can review.** Sampling is meaningful only against a defined population, and a store growing with traffic has no population, only a size. "We sample memory writes" then names an activity rather than a control.

**A memory store accumulates statements that were true when they were written.** Nothing retracts them. A position changes, a preference reverses or a matter closes, and the entry recording the earlier state sits beside the later one, unrelated. The read path needs a recency and conflict rule decided at design time: whether a newer entry supersedes or coexists, which one wins when two contradict and whether entries expire. Left undecided, the model resolves it per request, differently each time, and invisibly.

Scope, per user, per team or per organization, is a write-policy decision rather than a storage one, and the rule for choosing it is stated above. What the write policy adds is that **widening the scope is retroactive**: it republishes everything already written, including entries authored when the narrower boundary was the reason the user spoke freely. That is the change most likely to turn a convenience feature into a confidentiality event and the least likely to be treated as material, because no code path moves. Injected instructions that reached a write also survive into every later session in scope, the case in 4.12.

### Cross-user and cross-matter contamination

The failure is not exotic. It is the default behavior of a memory scoped more widely than the work.

| Scope | Legitimate content | The contamination risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Session** | Working state within one task | Effectively none. This is the safe default |
| **User** | Stated preferences, format choices, recurring context | A user's memory carrying facts about one client into work for another |
| **Team or matter** | Shared working context for a bounded engagement | Correct scope for professional services, and only if the boundary is enforced, not conventional |
| **Tenant or organization** | Organizational facts, terminology, policy | Cross-tenant leakage, which is a security incident and usually a contractual breach |
| **Global** | Nothing that came from a customer | Any customer-derived content here is a defect |

In legal and professional services this is not a privacy inconvenience, it is a conflicts and confidentiality question. A memory that carries facts from one matter into a system operating on another matter has crossed an ethical wall, and the fact that no human read the leaked content does not resolve it. ⚠ Whether a given memory design satisfies confidentiality and conflicts obligations is a professional-conduct determination and requires the firm's general counsel or risk function, not the architecture team.

Design consequences: memory keys must include the matter or client identifier and must be enforced at the storage layer rather than in the prompt; memory retrieval must be filtered by the same permission model as the primary corpus; and there must be a test in the eval set that attempts cross-scope retrieval and asserts it returns nothing.

### Memory versus retrieval versus fine-tuning

Three different answers to "the system should know this," routinely confused, with different economics on every axis that matters.

| | **Memory** | **Retrieval** | **Fine-tuning** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Answers** | "Remember what happened with this principal" | "Look this up in the corpus" | "Behave this way by default" |
| **Good for** | Continuity, preferences, working state across sessions | Facts, documents, current policy, anything with a source of record | Style, format, task-specific behavior, tone |
| **Bad for** | Facts of record. Memory has no authority and no version | Preferences and interaction history. Retrieval has no notion of a principal | Facts of any kind. Facts baked into weights cannot be updated, cited or deleted |
| **Update latency** | Immediate | Index refresh, minutes to hours | A training cycle, days to weeks |
| **Cost of deletion** | Moderate. Reaches the store plus any derived summaries | Moderate. Reaches chunks, embeddings, caches and logs | **Severe.** Deletion means retraining, and there is no partial erasure ⚠ |
| **Auditability** | Weak unless the write path is logged as a first-class event | Strong. The source is citable | Weakest. There is no source to cite |
| **Characteristic failure** | Stale or contaminated context asserted with confidence | Retrieval used where live state was needed | Facts trained in, then wrong and unremovable without a retrain |

**The decision rule: if it has a source of record, retrieve it; if it is about the principal rather than the world, remember it; and if it is a fact of any kind, never fine-tune it.**

The deletion row is the one that decides most enterprise cases. An erasure obligation over fine-tuned facts is satisfied only by retraining, which is why fine-tuning is a behavior tool and not a knowledge tool in any environment with data subject rights.

**Worked example, legal.** A firm enabled user-scoped memory across its research assistant. A partner working on two adverse matters found that the assistant referenced the opposing party's position from the first matter while drafting in the second. Nothing had leaked outside the partner, who was properly on both matters, so no confidentiality breach occurred. The firm still treated it as a control failure, correctly: the memory design made a breach possible for any user who was not on both matters, and no control prevented it. The remediation scoped memory to matter rather than user, added the matter identifier to the storage key, filtered memory retrieval through the matter access control list and added a cross-matter retrieval assertion to the eval set. Retention was set to the matter's retention period so that memory expires with the matter file rather than persisting independently.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question.** Who may write to the memory store, who has read what was written, and what evidences that the scope boundary held?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Choosing the write policy | Fixing a population that can be sampled, since an unbounded policy has a size rather than a population and cannot be reviewed | Memory write specification naming the admitted schema, the system owner |
| Setting the memory scope | Approving the contamination boundary as a confidentiality and conflicts decision, and re-approving before any widening, which republishes everything already written ⚠ | Scope decision record with the widening approval, the business system owner |
| Enabling the write path | Naming who may write and logging the write as a first-class event, without which memory has the weakest auditability of the three knowledge mechanisms | Write path owner and write log, the platform owner |
| Setting memory retention | Tying it to the retention period of the thing the memory is about rather than to a storage default | Retention schedule, the records function |

**What this costs the organization.** Review of memory writes is recurring and scales with traffic, and the schema-only policy buys its reviewability by refusing to remember what the schema did not anticipate. The forgotten cost is retroactive: widening the scope republishes entries authored when the narrower boundary was the reason the user spoke freely, and no code path moves, so nothing flags it as material.

**The executive translation.** Memory is a second store of regulated data with its own retention clock and its own conflicts exposure, and it is switched on by a product setting rather than by an architecture decision.

## 2.14 Build versus buy versus partner

The three options are genuinely different commitments and the mistake is treating the decision as a cost comparison. Cost is one of nine criteria and it is not the heaviest.

### The weighted framework

| Criterion | Weight | Favors build when | Favors buy when | Favors partner when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Differentiation** | 20 | This capability is why customers choose you | Everyone has it and nobody chooses on it | It is differentiating but not yours to own alone |
| **Data sensitivity** | 15 | The data cannot leave your boundary | The data is low sensitivity or the vendor is inside the boundary | A partner already holds it under an existing agreement |
| **Three-year total cost** | 15 | Volume is high enough that per-seat or per-call pricing dominates | Volume is modest or lumpy | Cost is shared with the partner's other clients |
| **Regulatory exposure** | 10 | You must evidence the control yourself | The vendor's attestations are accepted by your regulator | The partner carries the specialist obligation ⚠ |
| **Time to value** | 10 | You already have the platform and the team | You need it this quarter | The partner has the domain asset you would spend a year building |
| **Switching cost** | 10 | Lock-in would be severe | The interface is standard and the data is exportable | Contractually bounded |
| **Vendor viability** | 10 | The market is immature and vendors are unfunded | The vendor is established and the category is stable | The partner is a long-standing relationship |
| **Internal capability** | 5 | You have the team and can keep it | You do not, and hiring is not realistic | You have the domain and lack the engineering |
| **Exit cost** | 5 | Exit means shutting down a service you own | Exit means an export and a migration | Exit is a contract termination with defined data return |

Score each criterion 1 to 5 for each of the three options, multiply by weight and compare. The number is not the decision. The value is that the disagreement in the room relocates from "build or buy" to "is differentiation really a 5 here," which is a question with evidence behind it.

### A worked scoring, manufacturing

A manufacturer evaluating an assistant over maintenance manuals and service history for field technicians.

| Criterion | Weight | Build | Buy | Partner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Differentiation | 20 | 4 | 2 | 2 |
| Data sensitivity | 15 | 5 | 2 | 3 |
| Three-year cost | 15 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
| Regulatory exposure | 10 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| Time to value | 10 | 1 | 5 | 4 |
| Switching cost | 10 | 5 | 2 | 3 |
| Vendor viability | 10 | 5 | 2 | 3 |
| Internal capability | 5 | 2 | 5 | 4 |
| Exit cost | 5 | 4 | 3 | 3 |
| **Weighted total** | | **3.70** | **2.90** | **2.95** |

Build wins, driven by differentiation, data sensitivity and switching cost, with partner narrowly second on 2.95 against buy on 2.90, a gap too small to carry any weight, and the two weakest scores name the actual risk: time to value and internal capability. The correct output of this analysis is not "build" alone but "build, and the plan must address a slow start and a thin team," which is a materially better decision than a verdict.

### The heuristic and where it breaks

**Buy the commodity, build the differentiator, partner on the regulated.** It is a good first cut and it fails in four recognizable places.

| Break | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **When the commodity is the data path** | A commodity tool that requires your most sensitive corpus to leave your boundary is not a commodity decision. It is a data governance decision wearing a procurement costume, and the price comparison is irrelevant |
| **When the differentiator is not durable** | Building against a capability the model vendor will ship as a platform feature within a year produces an asset you maintain forever and nobody values. Test durability before invoking differentiation |
| **When partnering does not move accountability** | You remain accountable to your regulator and your customers regardless of who performs the work. Partnering distributes execution, not answerability ⚠ |
| **When internal capability is genuinely absent** | Building the differentiator with a team you cannot sustain produces an unmaintainable system, which is worse than buying an imperfect one. Capability is a precondition for build, not a criterion to be outweighed |

## 2.15 Production deployment architecture

Deploying a non-deterministic system breaks three assumptions that conventional release engineering rests on: that the same input produces the same output, that a diff between versions is meaningful and that the deployable artifact is code.

### Environments and the data problem

| Environment | Purpose | The AI-specific requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Development** | Individual iteration | Access to a representative subset of real data, or the prompt is tuned against fiction |
| **Integration** | Component wiring, contracts, tool behavior | Real tool endpoints in sandbox mode. Mocked tools hide the behaviors that matter most, which are error handling and retries |
| **Evaluation** | Running the eval sets against a candidate | **The environment most organizations lack.** It needs a production-shaped corpus and index, because retrieval quality cannot be evaluated against a toy corpus ⚠ Provisioning it usually requires a data-handling decision |
| **Staging** | Shadow and canary against live traffic | Production data path, production index, no user-visible output on the shadow path |
| **Production** | Serving | Per-request identity, trace identifiers, model identifier captured on every request |

The evaluation environment is where readiness is actually decided and it is routinely collapsed into staging. Separating them matters because the eval environment needs a frozen corpus so that scores are comparable across runs, and staging needs a live one so that behavior is real. Those are contradictory requirements and one environment cannot hold both.

### The four promotion gates

```
  PROMOTION PATH FOR A NON-DETERMINISTIC SYSTEM
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
   candidate release tuple
        |
   [ G1 EVAL ]      per-segment thresholds vs frozen sets
        |           plus self-disagreement baseline
        v
   [ G2 COST ]      cost per completed outcome at 1x and 3x
        |           volume, cache hit ratio verified
        v
   [ G3 SAFETY ]    harmful-output rate AND false-refusal rate,
        |           injection resistance, permission assertions
        v
   [ G4 OPERABILITY ] runbook current, owner named and agreed,
        |             rollback rehearsed, alerts wired
        v
   SHADOW (no user output) --> CANARY (slice) --> FULL
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Every gate is per segment. An aggregate pass hides a
  segment-level regression, which is how quality leaves quietly.
```

### Shadow and canary for non-deterministic systems

**Shadow deployment** runs the candidate on live traffic, discards its output and compares it to the incumbent's. **Canary** serves the candidate to a slice of real users. Both need adaptation, because you cannot compare outputs for equality.

| Adaptation | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Compare on graded metrics, not on diffs** | Two runs of the same version differ. A textual diff between versions carries almost no signal |
| **Establish a self-disagreement baseline first** | Run the incumbent against itself on the same inputs and measure how often the grader scores the two runs differently. That is your noise floor. Any candidate-versus-incumbent difference smaller than the noise floor is not a finding |
| **Use pairwise preference grading** | For generative outputs, a grader asked which of two outputs is better on a stated rubric is more sensitive than two independent absolute scores |
| **Size the shadow window by variance, not by time** | "Two weeks" is not a sample size. Compute what you need to detect the regression you care about, given the noise floor |
| **Watch the disagreement rate as its own signal** | A candidate that agrees with the incumbent 60 percent of the time and scores identically has changed behavior substantially. That is worth knowing before it reaches users, even if quality is flat |
| **Canary on a slice defined by segment, not by user hash** | A random hash slice may contain none of the segment where the regression lives. Slice deliberately across the segments your eval set names |

The self-disagreement baseline is the single most useful and least practiced technique in this section. Without it, teams read normal run-to-run variation as a regression, chase it and lose confidence in their own release process.

### Rollback when the artifact is a prompt and a model version

The deployable unit is not code. It is a tuple, and rollback means restoring all of it.

**The release tuple, seven fields:** prompt and system prompt version; model identifier and version; tool definitions and schemas; retrieval index version; routing and model-selection configuration; guardrail and policy configuration; eval set version the release was gated against.

Three rules follow.

1. **The tuple must be restorable without a deployment.** The readiness gate says the previous version must be restorable without a deploy, and for a tuple that means configuration-driven, not code-driven. A rollback that needs a release cycle is not a rollback, it is a fix.
2. **Partial rollback is a distinct and often correct operation.** Reverting the prompt while keeping the new index is legitimate and frequently the right response to a regression. The tuple must be independently addressable per field.
3. **The retrieval index is part of the tuple and is usually the field nobody versions.** An index rebuilt with new chunking is a behavior change of the same magnitude as a prompt change, and if it is not versioned the rollback restores the old prompt against the new index, which is a configuration nobody evaluated.

### Feature flags for AI behavior

Flags are the right mechanism and they carry a specific trap.

| Practice | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Flag the tuple fields, not the code paths** | The useful flags select model, prompt version, retrieval strategy, oversight placement and guardrail strictness |
| **Enumerate configurations, do not permit combinatorics** | Five independent boolean flags is thirty-two configurations, of which you have evaluated one. **A flag combination that has not been evaluated is an unevaluated system in production.** Ship named configurations, each with an eval result |
| **Flags that change oversight are governance changes** | A flag that disables a human gate is not a feature flag, it is a control change and needs the same approval as removing the control |
| **Every flag has an owner and an expiry** | Flags left permanently on become undocumented architecture. Expire them into the default or delete them |

### The release note a non-deterministic system requires

A conventional release note lists changes. For a system whose behavior is statistical, it must also state what is now different in distribution, and what nobody should be surprised by.

| Element | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **The tuple delta** | Which of the seven fields changed, from what to what |
| **Eval delta by segment** | Not a headline number. Per-segment scores before and after, with the segments named |
| **The noise floor** | The self-disagreement baseline, so a reader can tell which deltas are real |
| **Behavior changes users will notice** | Tone, length, format, refusal boundary, escalation rate. These generate the support tickets |
| **Known regressions accepted** | Segments that got worse and the reason the release proceeded. This is the consequences-accepted clause and it is the one that preserves credibility |
| **The rollback tuple and rehearsed restore time** | Exactly what will be restored and how long it takes |
| **What to watch, for how long** | The two or three metrics operations should monitor, the threshold that triggers a rollback and the date the heightened watch ends |

**Worked example, professional services.** A firm upgraded the model behind its research assistant. The eval delta was positive in aggregate, plus 4 points. The release note carried per-segment results and one segment, tax queries, was down 6 points against a noise floor of 2, which was a real regression. The release proceeded with the regression declared, the tax segment routed to the pinned prior model through the routing configuration and a two week watch on the tax escalation rate. Because the regression was in the release note, the tax practice raised no incident, the routing exception was visible in the dependency register with a removal date and the fix shipped three weeks later. The same regression on an aggregate-only release note would have surfaced as an angry practice head and an emergency rollback of everything.

## Solution Architecture: the one-page version

1. Four decisions organize a solution: ownership, shape, architecture, and a fourth bundling entry point, model tier, context strategy and delivery route. They are a diagnostic set, not a sequence, and the risk is mis-recognition rather than mis-ordering, because a delegation error upstream produces symptoms that look like architecture errors downstream.
2. Four behavior properties, four design consequences. Prediction means verification is architecture rather than quality assurance; fixed knowledge means everything current and proprietary is supplied; a hard context edge means context is curated and sized rather than accumulated; probabilistic steering means anything that must always hold is constrained in code rather than instructed. The properties do not announce themselves, so a system that ignores them drifts instead of erroring.
3. The platform map is three layers chosen by three different people for three different reasons: entry point for the user and the work, build-time interface for the engineering team, delivery route for the organization's cloud. "Can we use Claude" is three questions, and conflating them either kills a viable deployment or waves through a non-compliant one.
4. Seven primitives, seven jobs: tools act, MCP connects, subagents isolate and parallelize, hooks guarantee, skills package a procedure, agent teams coordinate peers, dynamic workflows compose at runtime. Select by naming the need rather than the technology, and hold the sharpest line in the set: hooks for deterministic guarantees, prompts for probabilistic guidance.
5. Three patterns, one dividing line. Augmented call, workflow or agent, and what separates them is whether the control flow lives in your code or inside the model. An agent is licensed only where the path cannot be enumerated and an unexpected output is both acceptable and recoverable, bound by constrained tool entry points, per-turn budgets, explicit permissions and stopping criteria.
6. Five workflow sub-patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. They combine rather than compete, and the right choice is the simplest one that meets the error tolerance and observability requirements, escalated only when measurement shows it falling short.
7. Multi-agent failure is asymmetric: subagent failures are recoverable and orchestrator failures often are not. Three things must be designed rather than assumed, decomposition, result structure and conflict resolution, and the pattern is justified only when the work genuinely exceeds one context.
8. Five reference architectures: agent, retrieval-augmented generation, document processing to evaluator-optimizer, ticket triage to routing, coding agent. Each carries its own eval contract, so composition doubles the maintenance surface and the eval surface at once. When in doubt, pick one.
9. Retrieval is for stable knowledge. Tool calls are for live state, meaning anything owned by a system and changing independently of your index. Answering order status from an index is a data-architecture failure, and a better embedding model, a shorter refresh interval and a higher similarity threshold are all the wrong fix.
10. Model selection is four criteria, capability, speed, cost and effort, and the characteristic error is over-selection rather than under-selection. Route a mixed workload instead of buying the hard minority's model for the easy majority, and treat every model fact as perishable.
11. Effort is a lever inside a chosen model, and tuning it is often a better move than switching models. Start efficiency-first and upgrade on a demonstrated capability gap, or capability-first and downgrade on demonstrated workflow optimization. Both exits require evidence.
12. Context strategy and context sizing are separate decisions that interact and do not determine each other. Four architectural questions give the monolithic baseline, the progressive window, the retrieval layer and the compaction policy; four platform mechanisms answer different token pressures, tool search for definitions, programmatic tool calling for round trips, caching for cost and context editing for stale results. Pick the one that matches where the tokens are actually going.
13. Prompts are versioned, owned and tested components, not a tuning activity. Aim at the right altitude between if-else logic in prose and guidance that assumes context you never supplied, climb the technique ladder from clear instruction and explicit criteria before reaching for extended thinking, and put any rule protecting money, identity or anything irreversible into code as a gate.
14. Caching is a reuse decision rather than a default. It pays where a stable prefix is re-sent often enough to amortize a write at a quarter over base input, or double at the one-hour lifetime, against reads at a tenth. Order the prompt stable-first, and note that changing a tool definition or the effort value invalidates everything after it.
15. Entry point, build-time interface and five delivery routes, with governance as a rule-out filter applied before cost and latency, never beside them. Residency, business associate agreement coverage, privilege and authorized-environment constraints eliminate routes outright, and a design costed before the route is checked is a design wasted.
16. An AI decision record adds seven clauses: model dependency, non-determinism tolerance, eval gate, oversight point, egress boundary, blast radius, and the reversal path with its switching condition.
17. Ask what happens when the component succeeds and is wrong, not only what happens when it fails.
18. Mandate three shared services and no more at first: gateway, identity and secrets, audit sink.
19. Share only when the interface is stable, defects mean the same thing everywhere and nobody is blocked. Otherwise let teams duplicate.
20. Never share eval sets, live prompts, business rules or corpora with different permission models.
21. Premature sharing kills adoption, and the platform then costs more than it saves. Name the queue tax out loud.
22. Pick the simplest model posture that meets your continuity obligation. Single vendor multi-model is right for most enterprises.
23. Abstract thin at the gateway. Thick vendor normalization costs the lowest common denominator, doubled evals and untested portability.
24. Every system has a vendor-set expiry date. Keep a dependency register with a named migration owner and a rehearsed fallback per system.
25. A pin without an expiry and an owner is a deferral. A fallback unexercised in six months is not a fallback.
26. Expect five regression classes on upgrade: format, verbosity, refusal boundary, tool behavior, prompt sensitivity. Gate every swap on a per-segment eval.
27. Five human placements: pre-action approval, post-action review, sampled audit, escalation on uncertainty, exception only. Only the first, fourth and fifth are preventive.
28. Post-action review is worthless without a real undo window. Sampled audit is a quality instrument, never a safety control.
29. Escalate on structural signals, never on uncalibrated self-reported confidence.
30. Reviewer capacity is finite. Route to a person where error is costliest: high value, ambiguous or contradictory sources, novel patterns, rights and entitlements, policy gaps.
31. Design against fatigue and automation bias: cap batches, no defaults, no bulk approve, isolate the claim.
32. Approval rate is uninterpretable without a base rate. Measure seeded-defect catch rate, override rate, time on task and escape rate.
33. The handoff package is six elements, and the most valuable one is what the system did not find.
34. Scope memory to the smallest useful principal, default to session and enforce the boundary at storage rather than in the prompt.
35. Retrieve facts, remember the principal, fine-tune only behavior. Deletion cost decides it.
36. Build versus buy versus partner is nine weighted criteria, not a cost comparison. Buy the commodity, build the differentiator, partner on the regulated and check the four places that breaks.
37. Partnering distributes execution and never distributes accountability.
38. Keep evaluation and staging as separate environments. One needs a frozen corpus, the other needs a live one.
39. Run four promotion gates per segment: eval, cost, safety, operability. Aggregate passes hide segment regressions.
40. Establish a self-disagreement baseline before reading any shadow or canary result. Below the noise floor is not a finding.
41. The deployable artifact is a seven-field tuple. Rollback restores the tuple without a deployment and per field.
42. Ship named flag configurations with eval results. An unevaluated flag combination is an unevaluated system in production.
43. The release note states the tuple delta, per-segment eval delta, the noise floor, user-visible behavior changes, accepted regressions, the rollback tuple and what to watch.
